items.title: Specific gravity and floating
items.reason: The density ratio to water is not a universal float/sink test in every fluid. Preserve the general fraction-submerged derivation and scope the specific-gravity shortcut to its water reference.

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id2036384">We use this last relationship to measure densities. This is done by measuring the fraction of a floating object that is submerged—for example, with a hydrometer. It is useful to define the ratio of the density of an object to a fluid (usually water) as <term id="import-auto-id3437631">specific gravity</term>:</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id2036384">We use this last relationship to measure densities. This is done by measuring the fraction of a floating object that is submerged—for example, with a hydrometer. It is useful to define the ratio of the density of an object to the reference density of water as <term id="import-auto-id3437631">specific gravity</term>:</para>

If an object floats, its specific gravity is less than one. If it sinks, its specific gravity is greater than one. Moreover, the fraction of a floating object that is submerged equals its specific gravity. If an object’s specific gravity is exactly 1, then it will remain suspended in the fluid, neither sinking nor floating. Scuba divers try to obtain this state so that they can hover in the water. We measure the specific gravity of fluids, such as battery acid, radiator fluid, and urine, as an indicator of their condition. One device for measuring specific gravity is shown in <link target-id="import-auto-id3063970"/>.</para>

items.title: Banked-curve normal force
items.reason: The sentence says banking reduces the normal force. For the ideal banked case developed next, N cos(theta) = mg, so N is larger than mg. Replace the claim with the role of its horizontal component.

items.title: Spring work: slow deformation and average force
items.reason: Action–reaction is valid for forces between the hand and spring; it is not a general argument that two forces on one object balance. State slow deformation and identify the average force in the work calculation. The area-under-the-graph and elastic-energy result remain unchanged.

passages.before_xml: <para id="eip-763">An <term id="isothermal">isothermal process</term> is a thermodynamic process in which no change in temperature takes place. A gas expanding isothermally, for example, does work on the surrounding, but its internal energy (as represented by the temperature) does not change, because enough heat flows in to balance out the energy expended in doing work. This is consistent with the first law of thermodynamics (<m:math><m:apply><m:eq/><m:cn>0</m:cn><m:mrow><m:ci>Δ</m:ci><m:ci>U</m:ci></m:mrow><m:apply><m:minus/><m:ci>Q</m:ci><m:ci>W</m:ci></m:apply></m:apply></m:math>, because <m:math><m:apply><m:eq/><m:ci>Q</m:ci><m:ci>W</m:ci></m:apply></m:math>). An isothermal process occurs if a thermodynamic process in a gas occurs slowly enough so that the gas remains in thermal equilibrium with the surrounding at all times.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="eip-763">An <term id="isothermal">isothermal process</term> is a thermodynamic process in which no change in temperature takes place. An ideal gas expanding isothermally, for example, does work on the surrounding, but its internal energy, which depends only on temperature, does not change, because enough heat flows in to balance out the energy expended in doing work. This is consistent with the first law of thermodynamics (<m:math><m:apply><m:eq/><m:cn>0</m:cn><m:mrow><m:ci>Δ</m:ci><m:ci>U</m:ci></m:mrow><m:apply><m:minus/><m:ci>Q</m:ci><m:ci>W</m:ci></m:apply></m:apply></m:math>, because <m:math><m:apply><m:eq/><m:ci>Q</m:ci><m:ci>W</m:ci></m:apply></m:math>). An isothermal process occurs if a thermodynamic process in a gas occurs slowly enough so that the gas remains in thermal equilibrium with the surrounding at all times.</para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737790371">How can we calculate the change in entropy for an irreversible process when <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>Δ</m:mn><m:msub><m:mi>S</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>tot</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub><m:mo stretchy="false">=</m:mo><m:mrow><m:mn>Δ</m:mn><m:msub><m:mi>S</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>h</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub><m:mo stretchy="false">+</m:mo><m:mn>Δ</m:mn><m:msub><m:mi>S</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>c</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ΔS rSub { size 8{"tot"} } =ΔS rSub { size 8{h} } +ΔS rSub { size 8{c} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is valid only for reversible processes? So we can calculate the change in entropy of the hot reservoir for a hypothetical reversible process in which 4000 J of heat transfer occurs from it; then we do the same for a hypothetical reversible process in which 4000 J of heat transfer occurs to the cold reservoir. This produces the same changes in the hot and cold reservoirs that would occur if the heat transfer were allowed to occur irreversibly between them, and so it also produces the same changes in entropy.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737790371">How can we calculate the change in entropy for irreversible heat transfer? This produces the same changes in the hot and cold reservoirs that would occur if the heat transfer were allowed to occur irreversibly between them, and so it also produces the same changes in entropy.</para>

items.title: Entropy of the system versus system plus surroundings
items.attention: Read closely: repeated scope correction across the section
items.reason: A system can lose entropy by releasing heat. The second-law statements must refer to an isolated system or to the combined system and surroundings. Coordinate the body, summary, and glossary; the numerical examples need no new results.

sources.locator: System versus surroundings entropy; reversible heat transfer

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169738182621">This result, which has general validity, means that <emphasis effect="italics">the total change in entropy for a system in any reversible process is zero.</emphasis></para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169738182621">This result, which has general validity, means that <emphasis effect="italics">the total change in entropy of the system and its surroundings in any reversible process is zero.</emphasis></para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169736590877">The entropy of various parts of the system may change, but the total change is zero. Furthermore, the system does not affect the entropy of its surroundings, since heat transfer between them does not occur. Thus the reversible process changes neither the total entropy of the system nor the entropy of its surroundings. Sometimes this is stated as follows: <emphasis effect="italics">Reversible processes do not affect the total entropy of the universe.</emphasis> Real processes are not reversible, though, and they do change total entropy. We can, however, use hypothetical reversible processes to determine the value of entropy in real, irreversible processes. The following example illustrates this point.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169736590877">The entropy of the system and that of its surroundings may each change, but their changes sum to zero for a reversible process. Sometimes this is stated as follows: <emphasis effect="italics">Reversible processes do not affect the total entropy of the universe.</emphasis> Real processes are not reversible, though, and they do change total entropy. We can, however, use hypothetical reversible processes to determine the value of entropy in real, irreversible processes. The following example illustrates this point.</para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737821042"><emphasis effect="italics">There is an increase in entropy for any system undergoing an irreversible process.</emphasis></para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737821042"><emphasis effect="italics">There is an increase in entropy for the system and its surroundings together during an irreversible process.</emphasis></para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737871583">With respect to entropy, there are only two possibilities: entropy is constant for a reversible process, and it increases for an irreversible process. There is a fourth version of <term id="import-auto-id1169737036046">the second law of thermodynamics stated in terms of entropy</term>:</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737871583">With respect to entropy, there are only two possibilities: the combined entropy of the system and its surroundings is constant for a reversible process and increases for an irreversible process. There is a fourth version of <term id="import-auto-id1169737036046">the second law of thermodynamics stated in terms of entropy</term>:</para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169738036913">Recall that the simple definition of energy is the ability to do work. Entropy is a measure of how much energy is not available to do work. Although all forms of energy are interconvertible, and all can be used to do work, it is not always possible, even in principle, to convert the entire available energy into work. That unavailable energy is of interest in thermodynamics, because the field of thermodynamics arose from efforts to convert heat to work.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169738036913">Recall that the simple definition of energy is the ability to do work. Entropy helps determine how much energy is unavailable to do work. Although all forms of energy are interconvertible, and all can be used to do work, it is not always possible, even in principle, to convert the entire available energy into work. That unavailable energy is of interest in thermodynamics, because the field of thermodynamics arose from efforts to convert heat to work.</para>
